strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation spanning four diverse benchmark collections (UCR-128, UEA-27, HAR, EEG) against a wide array of baseline families (self-supervised, statistical, tabular FMs, forecasting FMs, vision FMs, and TSFMs specialized for classification), with Mantis and its variants consistently achieving state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance.

The proposed multi-view Token Generator Unit (raw signal + first-order differential + patch-wise statistics) is well-motivated and its contribution is clearly validated via ablation (Figure 8), showing each branch adds discriminative value.

The layer-by-layer, epoch-by-epoch analysis (Section B.3) provides a genuinely interesting and non-trivial empirical finding: intermediate layers unlock the scaling benefits of contrastive pre-training while the final layer can overfit/stagnate. This finding is shown to generalize across other TSFMs (NuTime, MOMENT, TiRex, Chronos2), adding value beyond just Mantis itself.

Extensive and systematic ablations covering essentially every design decision (architecture components, kernel size, transformer variants, pre-training data source/size, augmentation choice, contrastive loss type, output-token aggregation, self-ensembling, predictor choice, adapters for multivariate data), which strengthens confidence in the reported gains and supports reproducibility.

Practical significance: the model is shown to be both accurate and highly lightweight/fast (Figures 4-5), making a credible case for deployment in compute-constrained settings, and the detailed complexity/runtime analysis is a useful contribution.

Good methodological care regarding evaluation validity, e.g., using synthetic pre-training data specifically to avoid train/test leakage with UCR/UEA, and the detailed TabPFN-vs-Mantis stratified comparison (Section C.3) that offers nuanced insight into when each model family excels.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the paper largely combines/adapts existing ideas (InfoNCE contrastive pre-training, RoPE/RMSNorm/SwiGLU transformer, synthetic pre-training via CauKer, intermediate-layer probing from Skean et al. 2025 and Roschmann et al. 2025, self-ensembling inspired by TiRex, cross-model fusion inspired by Roschmann et al. 2025) rather than introducing a single unifying new mechanism; the contribution reads more as a well-executed 'bag of tricks' than a fundamentally new method.

The magnitude of improvement from many individual test-time components is often modest (e.g., 0.5-1% from self-ensembling, output-token aggregation, or transformer variant choice), and the final competitive edge over strong baselines (TiRex, Chronos2, TiConvNext) on UCR is relatively small once multiple tricks are stacked, raising questions about how much of the gain is attributable to careful test-time engineering versus the core architecture/pre-training contribution.

The full enhanced pipeline (layer selection + token aggregation + self-ensembling + cross-model embedding fusion with a vision FM) adds considerable inference-time complexity and, when fused with large vision models like TiConvNext, undermines the 'lightweight' framing touted in the title/abstract for the best-performing configurations.

The 'zero-shot' terminology, while clarified early on, is actually linear-probing/feature-extraction with a classifier trained per downstream dataset; this framing could be considered misleading to readers skimming the abstract, especially given that fine-tuning results (which show large additional gains, Section C.1) are relegated to the appendix.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests) is reported when comparing Mantis to the closest competing baselines (e.g., TiConvNext, Chronos2) despite many accuracy differences being within 1-2 points and overlapping in some subgroups (e.g., UCR win-rate comparison with TabPFN/TabICL shown in Appendix D).

The explanation for why synthetic (CauKer) data outperforms real data of equal size relies mainly on a qualitative appeal to 'uniformity' from Wang & Isola (2020) without deeper quantitative analysis (e.g., explicit uniformity/alignment metrics comparing synthetic vs. real pre-training corpora).

The Impact Statement is extremely generic and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks (e.g., over-reliance on synthetic pre-training distributions for high-stakes domains like EEG/medical classification, or failure modes when domain shift from CauKer synthetic distributions is large).

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation spanning UCR (128 datasets), UEA (27 datasets), HAR (7 datasets) and EEG (11 datasets) collections, with numerous ablations (tokenizer branches, kernel size, transformer variant, pretraining data source, augmentation choice, contrastive loss variant, output-token aggregation, self-ensembling, cross-model fusion, adapters for multivariate data).

The resulting model is genuinely lightweight (2.2-4.2M parameters after/without pruning) and fast at inference, offering a favorable accuracy/compute trade-off compared to much larger forecasting- and vision-derived TSFMs, which is a useful practical contribution.

The layer-wise analysis showing that intermediate representations are more discriminative than final-layer embeddings, and that this behavior generalizes across several other TSFMs (NuTime, MOMENT, TiRex, Chronos2), is an interesting empirical observation with potential value beyond this specific model.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (dataset preprocessing, baseline configurations, package versions, hyperparameters), and an honest ablation showing where the proposed techniques do and do not help (e.g., SE-Mantis underperforming plain Mantis on the UCR-91 subset, output-token aggregation not helping at the last layer).
weaknesses: The paper's central 'zero-shot feature extraction' claim is questionable: for every foundation model (including competitors), the authors perform a per-dataset search over intermediate layers to pick 'a layer with the highest zero-shot performance.' It is not made fully clear whether this selection uses a held-out validation split or the test set itself; if the latter (or if validation data is scarce, as in many UCR datasets), this constitutes a form of test-time model selection/leakage that inflates all reported numbers and undermines direct comparability with prior published zero-shot results that do not perform such per-dataset tuning.

The array of test-time tricks (layer selection, token aggregation, self-ensembling, cross-model fusion) yields only marginal and inconsistent gains over plain Mantis (e.g., SE-Mantis 0.8582 vs Mantis 0.8584 on UCR-91 in Fig. 1; SE-Mantis helps on full UCR but not the 91-dataset subset), which weakens the motivation for the added complexity and calls into question the practical significance of the 'enhanced test-time methodology' as a core contribution.

Core novelty is somewhat limited: the synthetic pretraining data generator (CauKer) and the scalar patch encoder are both borrowed wholesale from other (concurrent/unpublished) works, and the token generator is an incremental combination of known ideas (conv patches, first-order differencing, NuTime-style scalar encoding). The main new ingredients are the specific combination and the test-time recipe, which is a narrower contribution than the framing suggests.

Fine-tuning results (Appendix C.1) show a large gap between zero-shot (~0.81-0.84) and fine-tuned (~0.85) performance, and other test-time-augmented FMs (TiRex, TiConvNext) are already highly competitive with plain Mantis, suggesting the 'new state-of-the-art' claim rests on a fairly narrow margin that could be sensitive to the evaluation protocol described above.

The Impact Statement is essentially a non-statement ('many potential societal consequences... none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), which is a weak treatment of limitations/ethics for a paper introducing a general-purpose foundation model intended for broad downstream deployment.

Some benchmark-specific hyperparameters (32 tokens, kernel size 41, resize length 512, choice of 3rd layer) appear tuned specifically to UCR, raising a mild concern about overfitting design choices to the primary benchmark rather than these being principled choices that would transfer to new domains without redoing the tuning.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation across four diverse benchmark collections (UCR-128, UEA-27, HAR, EEG) against a very large and well-chosen set of baselines (self-supervised, statistical, tabular FMs, forecasting FMs, vision FMs, classification FMs), with per-dataset results and multiple seeds reported.

Extensive, well-designed ablation studies covering the tokenizer branches, kernel size, transformer variants, pre-training data source/scale, contrastive loss/augmentation choice, layer-wise representation dynamics, output-token aggregation, self-ensembling, cross-model fusion, and predictor/normalization choices -- this level of ablation depth is unusually complete for a systems-style paper.

Practically relevant contribution: the model is shown to be both accurate and extremely lightweight/fast (2-4M parameters, runtime comparable to hand-crafted statistical features), which is a genuine advantage over the much larger vision/forecasting FMs compared against.

The observation that intermediate-layer representations, rather than the final layer, unlock scaling benefits of pre-training is an interesting and generalizable finding validated across several other TSFMs (NuTime, MOMENT, TiRex, Chronos2), adding value beyond the specific Mantis architecture.

Reasonable effort toward avoiding evaluation contamination by pre-training exclusively on synthetic (CauKer-generated) data, addressing a known criticism of prior TSFM pre-training corpora that overlap with UCR/UEA.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is modest: the token generator unit, contrastive InfoNCE pre-training, RoPE/RMSNorm/SwiGLU transformer blocks, and Random Crop Resize augmentation are all recombinations of well-established components rather than fundamentally new techniques; the primary contribution is careful engineering and thorough test-time optimization rather than a new algorithmic idea.

The paper selects the 'best' intermediate layer per model/dataset using zero-shot downstream performance ('we perform an intermediate layer analysis to determine a layer with the highest zero-shot performance'); if this selection uses test-set accuracy rather than a held-out validation split, this constitutes a form of test-set leakage that could optimistically bias absolute numbers for Mantis and all baselines alike, and the paper does not clearly describe a strict train/val/test protocol for this selection, which undermines the reliability of the reported accuracies.

Heavy reliance on CauKer (Xie et al., 2026), a concurrently unpublished/under-review synthetic data generator, for the entire pre-training pipeline raises reproducibility concerns if that resource is not yet fully available or stable, and the paper's central 'synthetic-only, no leakage' claim is only as strong as that external dependency.

Many of the reported performance gaps between top methods (e.g., Mantis vs. SE-Mantis vs. fused variants, or Mantis vs. TiConvNext/TiViT-H) are small (often <1-2%), and while per-run standard deviations are given for Mantis itself, there is no statistical significance testing across methods to substantiate that Mantis's ranking is robust rather than within noise.

The test-time pipeline (layer selection, token aggregation, multi-scale self-ensembling, cross-model fusion) adds substantial inference-time complexity and multiple design choices/hyperparameters (e.g., which interpolation lengths, which companion model to fuse with) that must be tuned per use case, partially offsetting the claimed 'lightweight' and 'simple zero-shot' appeal of the method.

Some baselines are not entirely comparable in spirit (e.g., TS2Vec/T-Loss/TNC learn per-dataset representations rather than being frozen universal encoders), and while the paper notes this, the headline claim of 'beating a very strong per-dataset self-supervised baseline' should be interpreted cautiously given the different problem setups.
